title: Why Should I Vex My Soul and Fret
description: Why Should I Vex My Soul and Fret in Tonic Solfa to ST. AGNES, doh is G: the solfa with the words, staff notation, 10 verses and a piano.
about: Isaac Watts wrote these words for The Psalms of David Imitated in the Language of the New Testament (1719): Psalm 37, part 1, headed “The cure of envy, fretfulness, and unbelief; or, The rewards of the righteous, and the wicked; or, The world's hatred, and the saint's patience”.
Watts' psalms were printed without tunes and sung to any tune of their metre, Common Metre (8.6.8.6). This page sets the words to ST. AGNES; any other Common Metre tune fits them as well.
underlay: Why should I vex my soul and fret To see the wi-cked rise? Or en-vy sin-ners wax-ing great, By vi-o-lence and lies.

lines: Why should I vex my soul and fret
As flowery grass cut down at noon,
So shall their glories vanish soon
Then let me make the Lord my trust,
So shall I dwell among the just,
I to my God my ways commit,
Thy hand, which guides my doubtful feet,
Fair as the light of dawning day,
The meek at last the earth possess,
And are the heirs of heav'n;
Rest in the Lord and keep his way,
Let sinners join to break your peace,
And plot, and rage, and foam;
The Lord derides them, for he sees
They have drawn out the threatening sword,
To slay the men that fear the Lord,
My God shall break their bows, and burn
Shall their own swords against them turn,

source: Isaac Watts, The Psalms of David Imitated (1719)
licence: Public domain: Isaac Watts died in 1748.
credits: Words by Isaac Watts (1674–1748), public domain; set to ST. AGNES by NoteFusion, as words-only hymn books were sung.
